title: Why Stale CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md Files Override Working Code in 90.1% of Runs (And the One-Sentence Fix)
author: Sean Kwon
summary: Instruction files like CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are usually written once when a repository sets up a coding agent and rarely touched again. Across 441 company repositories analyzed by Denisov-Blanch et al. (2026), 73.8% of AI configuration files were committed once and never modified. In a separate study of 356 public repositories by Treude and Baltes (2026), 23.0% of instruction files referenced code elements that no longer existed. When the codebase moves on while the instruction file stays frozen, coding agents receive two contradictory sources of truth. A study by Xiaonan Xu and Wenjing Wu from Georgia Tech and UC Boulder ( arXiv:2610.30571 ) measured what Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI do when CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md disagrees with the existing code across 320 runs on 40 Python projects. What Happened Across 320 Runs Without a Precedence Rule Each of the 40 Python projects in the study had working modules, a passing test suite, and an instruction file asking for one convention while the existing code used another across 16 convention categories (for example, print() versus logging , os.path versus pathlib , or string constants versus Enum ). Claude Code (v2.1.302 on Claude Sonnet 5.5) and Codex CLI (v0.163.0 on GPT-6 Sol) were asked to add a feature in 320 unattended runs totaling 720 convention choices. Without a precedence rule in the user-level instruction file: Across all 720 convention choices, 90.1% (649 of 720) followed the stale instruction file and only 4.2% followed the existing code (86.4% file adherence in Claude Code and 93.9% in Codex CLI). Claude Code explicitly noted the conflict between CLAUDE.md and the existing code in its final reply in 79 of 80 runs, yet still followed the stale file in 86.2% of its choices. Codex CLI went further in 20 of 80 runs: it rewrote the existing working modules to match the stale AGENTS.md file (removing a median of 198 lines across 9 existing files), which broke the project's original test suite in 17 of those 20 runs. Here is the exact kind of final reply Claude Code produced in the baseline condition after reading the code and seeing the mismatch: The existing concat.py, reader.py, writer.py and columns.py still use logging, pathlib, str.format() and absolute imports, which go against CLAUDE.md. Even after identifying that every module in the repository used logging and pathlib , the agent wrote the new feature using print() and os.path to obey CLAUDE.md . Why Coding Agents Rank a Stale File Above Working Code The study traces this behavior to how agent harnesses deliver context and how frontier models are trained to enforce the instruction hierarchy: Imperative phrasing: A line like Use print() for progress messages is written as a command, even when it was only meant to describe how the code looked when the line was written. Instruction-tier delivery: Claude Code injects CLAUDE.md directly after the system prompt inside a user message prefixed with IMPORTANT: These instructions OVERRIDE any default behavior and you MUST follow them exactly as written. Codex CLI wraps AGENTS.md inside an INSTRUCTIONS tag. Tool-output deprioritization: The actual source code only reaches the model when the agent calls a file-reading tool. Because frontier models are trained to rank system and user instructions above tool output to defend against prompt injection, an outdated rule in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md outranks the live code returned by the file reader. The One-Sentence Precedence Fix Because the conflict happens at the instruction layer, fixing it requires an instruction at the same layer. The authors added a single sentence to the user-level instruction file ( ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for Claude Code and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md for Codex CLI): When a repository's documentation and its existing code disagree, follow the conventions used in the existing code, and in your final reply point out each inconsistency you found between the documentation and the code. With that one sentence in place across the same 40 projects and 160 runs: The share of choices following the existing code jumped from 4.2% to 91.4% (658 of 720 choices), rising from 7.5% to 94.4% in Claude Code and from 0.8% to 88.3% in Codex CLI. Destructive rewrites of existing working modules by Codex CLI dropped from 20 runs to 0. The overall test pass rate across all 160 runs rose from 89.4% to 100% (with Codex CLI rising from 78.8% to 100%). Both agents reported the outdated rules in all 160 final replies so maintainers knew which lines in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md needed updating. Three Practical Steps to Stop Instruction Drift in Your Repositories You can combine the paper's user-level precedence rule with Claude Code's built-in instruction management features ( Claude Code Memory Docs ): 1. Add the precedence sentence to your global agent config Add the rule once to both user-level files so it applies to every repository you open: cat << 'EOF' >> ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md When a repository 's documentation and its existing code disagree, follow the conventions used in the existing code, and in your final reply point out each inconsistency you found between the documentation and the code. EOF cat << ' EOF ' >> ~/.codex/AGENTS.md When a repository' s documentation and its existing code disagree, follow the conventions used in the existing code, and in your final reply point out each inconsistency you found between the documentation and the code. EOF 2. Share one root file across Claude Code and Codex Maintaining separate CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files in the same repository doubles the chance that one file goes stale after a refactor. Keep your shared build commands and architecture rules in AGENTS.md , and import it from CLAUDE.md using the @path syntax: @AGENTS.md ## Claude Code Use plan mode for changes under `src/billing/` . Alternatively, configure Claude Code to load both CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md automatically in ~/.claude/settings.json : { "pluginConfigs" : { "cc-plugin-agents-md@builtin" : { "options" : { "instructionFiles" : "claude-md-and-agents-md" } } } } 3. Move directory-specific conventions into path-scoped rules and run /doctor prompt-audit Root instruction files go stale fastest when they try to document file-level conventions for every subfolder. In Claude Code, place directory-specific rules in .claude/rules/*.md with a paths glob in the YAML frontmatter so they load on demand only when the agent reads or edits matching files: --- paths: - "src/api/**/*.ts" --- # API Handler Conventions - Validate request bodies with the schema helpers in `src/api/validators/` . - Return structured errors through `sendApiError()` . When you upgrade dependencies or finish a migration, run /doctor prompt-audit inside a Claude Code session (available in v2.1.283 or later) to scan CLAUDE.md , AGENTS.md , .claude/rules/ , and .claude/skills/ for references to deleted files, missing commands, and conflicting instructions before they steer your next session.

title: Detecting Flaky Tests and Finding Their Root Causes with Strands Agents and Gemini
author: Alicia Marianne Gonçalves
summary: A few years ago (three years at most), one of the biggest challenges QA Engineers faced was: how do we convince the business and the team that we should invest in automated tests? Today, with AI, this issue has been mostly solved. We don't spend much time coding automated tests because we have AI to do it for us, but a new challenge appears: flaky tests . In this article, I will explain what a flaky test is, how I built a tool to help identify them, and how I used AI to run a first analysis. What Is a Flaky Test and Why It Matters Before going into more detail about the solution, let's understand what a flaky test is and why we should worry about it. In a few words, a flaky test is an automated test that produces both passing and failing results without any change to the code or to the test itself. If they pass, why should we monitor them? In the end, they pass. That may be your first thought, but once you understand what a flaky test is, you see that in big projects it can hurt the team's trust in their own product and tests, real failures start being ignored, and the CI time and cost per pipeline go up. Quick overview of the project Based on these concerns, I developed this project. The code is available on GitHub: flaky-test-detector . In the first draft, I planned only to parse the test results, score them per test and commit, and do the analysis manually: After this first draft, I thought: why not integrate an AI to help me with the analysis? With this in mind, I added new features to support the analysis and the integration with AI models. Today, the solution looks like this: The project is organized like this: flaky-test-detector/ ├── .github/workflows/ │ └── flaky-report.yml # weekly analysis + result files ├── agents/ │ └── agent.py # optional AI agent: root-cause analysis of reports ├── docs/ │ └── how-it-works.svg # diagram used in this README ├── flaky_detector/ │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── __main__.py # CLI │ ├── parsers.py # JUnit XML parser │ ├── github.py # fetches JUnit artifacts from GitHub Actions │ ├── scoring.py # flakiness scoring and ranking │ └── report.py # result files (JSON / CSV / Markdown) ├── scripts/ │ └── generate_junit.py # generates sample JUnit XML files ├── results/ # sample JUnit XML files (git-ignored) ├── reports/ # generated reports and AI analyses ├── tests/ ├── pyproject.toml # project metadata and dev dependencies (uv) ├── requirements.txt └── README.md Scoring and Ranking the Flaky Tests Let's understand how the project scores and ranks the flaky tests. It starts by receiving a JUnit report in XML format (a standard output of most test frameworks, with one <testcase> per executed test), and parsers.py is responsible for parsing the information in this file into the proper format: class Outcome ( str , Enum ) : PASSED = "passed" FAILED = "failed" ERROR = "error" SKIPPED = "skipped" @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class TestResult : """A single test execution in a single CI run.""" __test__ = False # keep pytest from trying to collect this class name : str # "<classname>::<name>" outcome : Outcome commit_sha : str | None run_id : str | None time : float = 0.0 message : str | None = None source : str | None = None # file the result came from @property def passed ( self ) -> bool : return self . outcome is Outcome . PASSED If the file isn't a valid JUnit XML, an exception is raised; if it is valid, the parsing proceeds. When scoring.py is called, it uses the FlakinessScorer class, which is responsible for taking the TestResult objects and turning them into TestScore objects. Each result is grouped by test name and then by commit, and for each (test, commit) pair the scorer checks the outcome. It ignores: skipped tests, since they say nothing about flakiness; results from JUnit files without the commit_sha property (the commit id), since they can't be compared with each other. Both failed and error count as a failure. @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class TestScore : """Flakiness score of a single test.""" __test__ = False # keep pytest from trying to collect this class name : str commits : int # commits with usable data for this test flaky_commits : int # commits where the test had mixed outcomes commits_where_flaky : tuple [ str , . . . ] = field ( default = ( ) ) error_messages : tuple [ str , . . . ] = field ( default = ( ) ) # distinct failure messages, first seen first @property def score ( self ) -> float : return self . flaky_commits / self . commits if self . commits else 0.0 class FlakinessScorer : def score ( self , results : Iterable [ TestResult ] ) -> list [ TestScore ] : outcomes : dict [ str , dict [ str , set [ bool ] ] ] = defaultdict ( lambda : defaultdict ( set ) ) messages : dict [ str , dict [ str , None ] ] = defaultdict ( dict ) # ordered, de-duplicated for r in results : if not r . commit_sha or r . outcome . value == "skipped" : continue outcomes [ r . name ] [ r . commit_sha ] . add ( r . passed ) if not r . passed and r . message : messages [ r . name ] [ r . message ] = None scores = [ ] for name , by_commit in outcomes . items ( ) : flaky = tuple ( sorted ( sha for sha , seen in by_commit . items ( ) if len ( seen ) > 1 ) ) scores . append ( TestScore ( name = name , commits = len ( by_commit ) , flaky_commits = len ( flaky ) , commits_where_flaky = flaky , error_messages = tuple ( messages [ name ] ) , ) ) return scores The script marks a test as flaky when, for the same commit, the outcomes are both {True, False} : the test failed and passed with the same code base. It then generates the data that the Ranker needs, in the following format: { "name" : "tests.checkout.test_cart::test_9" , "commits" : 10 , "flaky_commits" : 3 , "commits_where_flaky" : [ "gen0007d154385" , "gen05893e77ff9" , "gen059095256f8" ] , "error_messages" : [ "AssertionError: timeout waiting for gateway" , "ConnectionError: connection reset by peer" ] } When the FlakinessRanker class is called, it uses this data to rank the tests. It only considers tests with data from at least 5 commits ( min_commits ), so the score can be trusted, and it flags a test as flaky when its score is 0.1 or higher ( threshold ). Both values can be changed: def __init__ ( self , threshold : float = 0.1 , min_commits : int = 5 ) -> None : if not 0.0 <= threshold <= 1.0 : raise ValueError ( "threshold must be between 0 and 1" ) if min_commits < 1 : raise ValueError ( "min_commits must be >= 1" ) self . threshold = threshold self . min_commits = min_commits The score is the total of flaky_commits (the number of commits where the same test passed and failed) divided by the total of commits available for that test in the pipeline. One test ran on 10 commits, and on 3 of them it both passed and failed on the same commit. For this example, commits is 10 and flaky_commits is 3, so the score is 0.3. With this first implementation, we can already see the first results. I created some JUnit reports and, after running the command below, I got this output: python -m flaky_detector analyze ./results/*.xml --threshold 0.1 Each line shows the score, the test name and the number of flaky commits out of the commits with data for that test. Reports and Agent Creation As I mentioned before, after the basics I thought: why not improve it? The first step was creating reports of the results. Since I was already thinking about integrating an AI agent, the report needed a format that suits it well. The report is created by report.py , in JSON, CSV and Markdown formats (using the --output-dir option). In this article, we will focus on the JSON format, since it is the one used by the AI agent: { "generated_at" : "2026-11-10T19:32:23+00:00" , "source" : "local" , "threshold" : 0.1 , "min_commits" : 5 , "results_parsed" : 19644 , "tests_analyzed" : 109 , "flaky_count" : 12 , "flaky_rate" : 0.1101 , "tests" : [ { "name" : "tests.checkout.test_cart::test_9" , "score" : 0.7 , "commits" : 60 , "flaky_commits" : 42 , "is_flaky" : true , "commits_where_flaky" : [ "gen0007d154385" , "gen059095256f8" ] , "error_messages" : [ "AssertionError: timeout waiting for gateway" , "ConnectionError: connection reset by peer" , "AssertionError: race condition on shared state" , "AssertionError: expected 200, got 503" , "TimeoutError: operation timed out after 30s" ] } ] } To build the AI agent, I used the Strands Agents SDK . My first contact with this SDK was at the Train the Trainers workshop (thank you, AWS EMEA, for the invite), and since the way to configure the agent is very simple, I decided to use it in this project. In this project I am using GeminiModel (the API key is read from the GOOGLE_API_KEY variable in .env ), but you can switch to a different model; see Model Providers . from strands import Agent from strands . models . gemini import GeminiModel model = GeminiModel ( client_args = { "api_key" : api_key } , model_id = "gemini-2.5-flash" , ) agent = Agent ( model = model , tools = [ fetch_json_report , export_analysis ] , name = "Flaky Test Analysis Agent" , description = "This agent analyzes flaky test reports and provides insights on flaky tests, their scores, trends, and it analyzes the error messages to provide insights on the root causes of flakiness. And when it is asked to summarize the flaky test report, it will use the fetch_json_report tool to retrieve the report data and then provide a summary of how many tests are flaky and which are the worst and the possible root causes based on the error messages." , system_prompt = "You are a helpful assistant that analyzes flaky test reports. Use the fetch_json_report tool to retrieve report data when needed. Always read the error_messages of each flaky test and infer the possible root causes (timeouts, race conditions, network/gateway instability, shared state, etc.), saying which tests each cause affects and how confident you are. After you finish analysing, call export_analysis once with summary, root_causes and recommendations to save the Markdown report, then tell the user the file path." , ) When building an agent, we need to provide it with tools so it can do its job. For this app, I created two tools: fetch_json_report : fetches the generated JSON reports. It is responsible for finding the files based on a timestamp or a period and returning them in a single response, ordered from oldest to newest. export_analysis : saves the analysis made by the AI in a Markdown file. With this, it is possible to call the agent to run the analysis: def main ( ) -> None : parser = argparse . ArgumentParser ( description = "Analyze flaky test reports with an AI agent." ) parser . add_argument ( "period" , nargs = "?" , default = "last_24_hours" , choices = list ( PERIODS ) , help = "period of reports to analyze (default: %(default)s)" ) args = parser . parse_args ( ) label = args . period . replace ( "_" , " " ) agent ( f "Summarize the flaky test reports from the {label} (period={args.period}): " "how many tests are flaky and which are the worst? After finishing, analyze the error messages to infer the possible root causes of flakiness and give recommendations to fix them. And create the report file with export_analysis tool, then tell me the path of the Markdown file that was written." ) if __name__ == "__main__" : main ( ) The period is passed as an argument (for example, python agents/agent.py last_7_days ), and the agent provides a report like this one: Flaky Tests Analysis - Last 24 Hours . What Can Be Done With This Ok, now it is possible to identify flaky tests and even analyze them. What can I do with this? First, you can start implementing it in your team. Monitoring your tests and flagging the flaky ones can help you improve the team's trust in what they are building, reduce CI costs, and avoid real bugs being ignored because the test passes on the second or third execution. When should you run this? It depends on how your team works: If your team has continuous deployment, and deploys every day or every week, it is interesting to run this once per week. It can also help if you have problems merging PRs in lower environments, to understand what is happening. If you don't have continuous deployment and deploy once per month, my recommendation is to run this on every deployment, always comparing the latest executions to see whether the number increased or not. The AI analysis is optional. You can run just the Score and Rank steps and, at the end of a cycle, a month or even a quarter, use the agent to give you feedback. Limitations and Integrations Today, the JUnit XML file must have the property <property name="commit_sha" value=""/> (the commit id) and the property <property name="run_id" value=""/> . Since the solution was built with GitHub Actions in mind, it may need changes for other frameworks and pipelines. When the results are fetched from GitHub Actions ( --repo ), both values are taken from the GitHub run itself. There is already a workflow to integrate with GitHub Actions ( .github/workflows/flaky-report.yml ). It runs every Monday, generates the reports and uploads them as an artifact. If you plan to add it to your own workflow, it may need adjustments, and the analyzed repository must publish its JUnit XML files as workflow artifacts. For the AI model, you can set up your favorite one. Remember to check Model Providers to adapt it to your context. Another suggestion is to integrate with a reporting tool, like Grafana, so you can see the behavior of your flaky tests at different points in time and whether they are decreasing or not. Conclusion Flaky tests are not just an annoyance: they erode the team's trust in the tests and hide real failures. Measuring them is the first step to dealing with them, and a simple score per test and commit is enough to get started. The AI analysis gives you a first look at the possible root causes, but it doesn't replace a human reviewing the results, since failures caused by the infrastructure can also look like flakiness. Give it a try and see how your own pipeline behaves!

title: HunterX Just Got Smarter. A Lot Smarter.
author: ahmed Awad (Nullc0d3)
summary: What if a security assessment engine could do more than discover vulnerabilities? What if it could question its findings, recover from execution failures, understand threat models, visualize attack paths, and follow a structured offensive security methodology? That's exactly the direction I'm taking with HunterX. I'm excited to share a major set of upgrades that brings HunterX closer to what I envision as a truly AI-directed autonomous security assessment engine. This isn't simply about adding more tools or running more scans. It's about making the entire assessment process smarter, more adaptive, more evidence-driven, and more reliable. Here's what's new. 🔥 What's New in HunterX? Multi-Agent Consensus Reviewer Finding a potential vulnerability is one thing. Being confident that it's real is another. I've introduced a configurable BaseReviewer interface, along with SimpleMockReviewer, to support evidence-chain review and improve finding confidence. The objective is to reduce false positives and make evidence validation a more meaningful part of the assessment lifecycle. Self-Healing Debugger Tool failures shouldn't necessarily mean the end of an assessment. With DebuggerAgent integrated into MissionExecutor, HunterX can now analyze tool execution errors, identify potential causes, and attempt retries using corrected parameters. The goal is to make mission execution more resilient without compromising scope enforcement, authorization, or security policies. An autonomous engine should know how to handle failure, not simply report it. Threat Modeling Integration Security testing should be driven by more than a list of discovered endpoints. I've added: ThreatModelParser ThreatModelIntegrator These components bring structured threat models, including STRIDE, into mission planning. HunterX can use threat-model context to identify gaps between theoretical threats and the security tests actually performed. This introduces a more structured, threat-driven approach to assessment coverage. Attack Path Visualization Individual findings don't always tell the complete story. Sometimes, the real security impact becomes clear only when multiple weaknesses and relationships are connected. The new AttackPathVisualizer, integrated into the correlation module, enables knowledge-graph exports in visualization-ready JSON formats. This helps make attack paths, evidence relationships, and security analysis easier to understand and communicate. Offensive Security Doctrine Plugin This is one of the additions I'm particularly excited about. I've introduced an internal plugin called: skill_offensive_doctrine Its purpose is to bring structured, professional offensive security methodology directly into HunterX. It includes: Dedicated HUNT MODE / DOCTRINE ON activation. Live assessment context through hunterx state. Specialized modes for RECON, WEB, API, LLM, MOBILE, SOURCE CODE, EXPLOITATION, and REPORTING. TRIAGE and CHAIN workflows. An ONLY QUESTION gate. Engagement-type enforcement. A Kill List and 17 Critical Rules. Evidence Discipline, marker discipline, body-diff analysis, and statistical sampling. Reconnaissance pipelines and canonical attack chains. Web3 Immunefi assessment knowledge. LLM agent injection taxonomy. Security research patterns covering 2024–2026, including the SAML wave. Impact-first offensive security writeups. And importantly, the plugin follows a zero-break architecture: opt-in, isolated, and fully rollbackable. It's designed to provide methodology and context without replacing HunterX's underlying execution and security controls. 🧪 Capability Verification Matrix One thing I strongly believe in: A feature shouldn't be considered complete simply because its code exists. It should be verifiable. That's why I've also added a formal Capability Verification Matrix. It covers: Consensus Reviewer: reviewer disagreement and false-positive testing. Self-Healing Debugger: failure recovery and bounded retries. Threat Modeling: STRIDE coverage and gap analysis. Attack Path Visualizer: graph integrity and evidence provenance. Offensive Doctrine: activation, isolation, rollback, and policy enforcement. The complete verification matrix is available at: tests/capability_verification/capability_verification_matrix.md This gives the new capabilities a dedicated verification structure rather than relying on feature descriptions alone. 📊 Reporting and Evidence HunterX continues to support multiple reporting and evidence formats: Markdown — Human-readable reports. HTML — Visual security dashboards. JSON — Machine-readable results. SARIF 2.1 — Integration with VS Code and GitHub CodeQL workflows. PDF — Professional document exports. Evidence Package (ZIP) — Bundled assessment evidence. The guiding principle remains the same: Every finding should have traceability to observations, evidence, validation, proof, replay, impact, tool results, target intelligence, or explicit analyst reasoning. 🌍 HunterX Is Already Part of the Security Community I'm also proud to see HunterX listed and featured in several well-known cybersecurity and open-source discovery resources: OWASP Community – Vulnerability Scanning Tools: https://owasp.org/www-community/Vulnerability_Scanning_Tools Awesome: https://awesome.re/ Awesome Red Teaming: https://github.com/0xMrNiko/Awesome-Red-Teaming Awesome AI in Cybersecurity: https://github.com/ElNiak/awesome-ai-cybersecurity These listings are an encouraging milestone for the project and a great motivation to keep pushing its development forward. HunterX also supports Linux, macOS, and Windows. 🧠 The Bigger Picture My vision for HunterX has never been to build another vulnerability scanner. I want to build an engine that can: Observe → Reason → Test → Validate → Prove → Correlate → Reassess → Report. An engine where AI provides strategic direction, while the execution layer enforces scope, authorization, safety, and evidence integrity. An engine that doesn't just tell you what might be vulnerable, but works toward establishing what is actually vulnerable, why it matters, and what evidence supports that conclusion. There's still a lot to build, improve, and validate. That's part of the journey. But every iteration brings HunterX closer to that vision. 🚀 Explore HunterX Official Website: https://nullc0d30.github.io/HunterX/ GitHub Repository: https://github.com/nullc0d30/HunterX PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/hunterxsec/ Docker: nullc0d30/hunterx - Docker Image Created and maintained by Ahmed Awad (NullC0d3). If you're working in Cybersecurity, Threat Intelligence, Penetration Testing, Red Teaming, or AI-driven Security Research, I'd genuinely love to hear your thoughts. title: E-Commerce Recovery Control: Background Job Queue Admission After Seven Delayed Retry Days
author: IgnazCole6453
summary: A rate-limited worker pool changes the scheduling question. If a large e-commerce background job queue backlog becomes eligible at once, admitting every delayed retry can recreate the overload that caused it. Short answer: keep retry eligibility in a durable ledger, let cron wake a bounded dispatcher, and enqueue only the work the pool can absorb. The queue should own ready work, while the ledger owns waits that exceed the queue's delayed-message limit. The evaluation constraint is operational recovery: after dispatch resumes, the oldest valid job must get younger without saturating the workers or repeating an expensive side effect. A simple delayed timer can pass a timing test and still fail that recovery test. I don't count an enqueue acknowledgment as success; for AI-generated catalog work, the output also has to pass the same schema and content evals as a first attempt. That distinction matters. Start with recovery invariants, not a longer timer Imagine a catalog enrichment pool paused while supplier data is unavailable. Product records continue to accumulate retry dates, and some dates are weeks away. When those records become due, the system has two jobs: preserve the intended eligibility time and control how quickly due work returns to service. A queue delay handles the first only while the delay remains inside its supported window. It does not, by itself, solve the second. The tempting approach is to split a long wait into a chain of shorter delayed messages. That creates ambiguous state. A product can change revision during the chain; an operator can pause the campaign; a message can be delivered more than once; and the worker pool can still receive the entire cohort at the final boundary. Each hop also makes it harder to answer a basic recovery question: which records are due but have not yet been offered? Use explicit invariants instead: A stable job ID identifies the logical side effect across every offer. next_attempt_at is durable application state, not an in-memory timer. The dispatcher admits no more than its current budget on one tick. A product revision is either pinned or rejected as superseded by an explicit policy. Completion is checked before the costly dependency is called. These rules do not promise exactly-once execution across a database and a queue. They make repeated offers harmless, which is the useful contract when claiming a database record and publishing a message cannot share one transaction. How should a background job queue run scheduled retry after a delayed message limit? Use two time horizons. For short waits that fit the queue's documented delayed-delivery window, native delay keeps the system small. For waits beyond that boundary, store a retry row with a stable ID, eligibility timestamp, attempt count, revision, state, and lease. A periodic trigger invokes a dispatcher; it does not become the clock of record. The dispatcher atomically claims a limited group of eligible rows. Each claim has an expiry so an interrupted invocation does not strand work forever. It then publishes the stable ID and immutable execution inputs to the ready queue. Once an offer is recorded, the normal worker path takes over. Concern Owner Recovery rule Long-horizon eligibility Retry ledger Persist the date independently of queue retention Release rate Dispatcher Claim no more than current worker headroom Duplicate offer Worker and completion store Reuse the stable ID and skip completed effects Changed catalog input Application policy Pin the revision or mark the old request superseded Generated result quality Eval harness Apply normal schema and content checks after retry There is a subtle boundary here. Cron is allowed to run twice, arrive late, or overlap with another invocation because correctness comes from atomic claims and idempotent work. The schedule controls how often capacity is reconsidered; it must not determine whether a record exists. This is why a cron-only design, where the job list lives in configuration, becomes awkward as soon as operators need per-record cancellation, inspection, or rescheduling. Keep classification ahead of scheduling too. A temporary rate-limit response can move next_attempt_at . Invalid product input should become terminal or enter review. Giving malformed input a longer clock turns a data-quality problem into future load, and no retry mechanism fixes that. A small Python controller is enough to test the contract The application may create background jobs from Node.js; the controller below is Python because the scheduling contract is language-neutral and fits cleanly into the same eval harness used for the catalog pipeline. It deliberately contains no vendor route or SDK. from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import datetime , timedelta from typing import Protocol @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class DueJob : job_id : str product_id : str product_revision : int attempt : int class RetryLedger ( Protocol ) : def claim_due ( self , * , now : datetime , limit : int , lease_until : datetime , ) -> list [ DueJob ] : . . . def mark_offered ( self , * , job_id : str , offered_at : datetime ) -> None : . . . def release_claim ( self , * , job_id : str ) -> None : . . . class ReadyQueue ( Protocol ) : def enqueue ( self , * , key : str , payload : dict [ str , object ] ) -> None : . . . def dispatch_due_jobs ( ledger : RetryLedger , queue : ReadyQueue , * , now : datetime , admission_budget : int , ) -> int : jobs = ledger . claim_due ( now = now , limit = admission_budget , lease_until = now + timedelta ( minutes = 5 ) , ) offered = 0 for job in jobs : try : queue . enqueue ( key = job . job_id , payload = { "job_id" : job . job_id , "product_id" : job . product_id , "product_revision" : job . product_revision , "attempt" : job . attempt , } , ) except TimeoutError : ledger . release_claim ( job_id = job . job_id ) continue ledger . mark_offered ( job_id = job . job_id , offered_at = now ) offered += 1 return offered The five-minute lease is example configuration, not throughput advice. Set it from measured publish latency and invocation behavior, then test expiry with a fake clock. I'm not sure a fixed cron interval is right for every store; burst shape, recovery deadline, downstream limits, and oldest-due age are the evidence needed to choose it. My notebook-sized fixture would seed five rows: three due, one due tomorrow, and one complete. With an admission budget of two, the first tick must offer two due rows. A repeated tick must not repeat either completed side effect. Next, expire a claim before mark_offered , advance the clock, and verify that the same stable ID becomes eligible for another offer. Finally, change one product revision while its retry is waiting and assert the chosen supersession policy. That last case catches an expensive mistake. Queue mechanics can be perfectly correct while an old generation request overwrites newer catalog input. Record token use by stable job ID and attempt, and run output evals after every execution; otherwise duplicate offers and low-quality retries disappear inside an apparently healthy throughput chart. Drain the backlog as a feedback loop An admission budget should respond to observed headroom, not to the number of due rows alone. Start a recovery drill with a low limit, observe worker saturation and completion, then raise or hold the next release. Fresh orders may need a reserved share of capacity so a historical catalog backlog cannot monopolize the pool. Fairness can also require ordering by eligibility time rather than repeatedly selecting newer, easier jobs. The primary progress signal is the age of the oldest eligible record. Pair it with accepted outputs per attempt, worker utilization, claims per tick, lease expirations, duplicate suppression, terminal input failures, and token use. Queue depth is secondary: a deep queue can be draining normally, while a shallow queue can hide one job that has been skipped for days. Go slowly. Before copying this design, run a controlled drill: pause dispatch, accumulate due records, resume with a small budget, invoke the dispatcher twice, interrupt once between enqueue and mark_offered , and supersede one product revision. The pass condition is not merely that messages move. Oldest-due age must fall, the pool must remain under its chosen saturation boundary, completed effects must not repeat, and regenerated content must still clear the eval suite. The catch is the durable-ledger design adds a state model, atomic claiming, lease cleanup, dashboards, and an idempotency contract shared by producers and workers. It is not suitable when the team cannot operate those semantics. Stick with native delayed delivery when every wait fits the supported window and there is no need for independent inspection or paced recovery. A durable workflow system is another reasonable category when long waits and resumable steps are central, but it brings its own execution model and operational surface. Choose from the recovery evidence. A cron-triggered ledger earns its complexity only when a rehearsal shows that bounded admission, explicit state, and stable IDs solve a problem the ready queue cannot express alone. title: The Filesystem Your Multi-GPU Rig Actually Needs
author: Amirhossein Ghanipour
summary: You install four PCIe Gen5 NVMe drives in a multi-GPU server, bring up eight H100s, launch torchrun , and notice an irritating pattern: GPU utilization fluctuates between 40% and 95%. A quick look at nvidia-smi suggests that the GPUs are waiting for data. Profiling shows that CPU time is being spent not only on preprocessing, but also on filesystem activity: metadata operations, lock contention, and page-cache writeback during checkpointing. In a modern deep-learning system, the filesystem is not merely a passive storage layer. It is part of the data pipeline, and its concurrency characteristics can affect end-to-end training throughput. This article looks at two common local-storage workloads: Parallel data ingestion: dozens of PyTorch DataLoader workers issue concurrent reads and metadata requests. Large checkpoint writes: training processes serialize model weights, optimizer states, and tensor data into files that can range from 10 GB to more than 200 GB per rank. For these workloads, XFS is often a strong choice for local NVMe scratch storage. Its allocation-group architecture, extent-based allocation, and delayed allocation can make it scale well under concurrent access. That does not mean XFS wins every workload or that filesystem choice alone fixes an input pipeline; the data layout, access pattern, kernel, mount options, and hardware all matter. At a glance Workload or concern Why it matters XFS characteristics Many concurrent readers Workers compete for metadata and I/O resources Allocation groups allow metadata work to be distributed Large sequential writes Checkpointing can interrupt training Extent-based allocation and delayed allocation help produce large contiguous allocations Millions of tiny files Metadata operations can dominate useful I/O XFS is capable, but a sharded dataset is usually a better architectural solution Copy-on-write workloads Shared extents can add write and metadata overhead when modified Ordinary XFS writes are in-place; reflink-shared extents use CoW NVMe throughput Queueing and I/O size affect achievable bandwidth XFS can scale well, but device and workload tuning still matter 1. The concurrency problem PyTorch's torch.utils.data.DataLoader can run multiple worker processes using num_workers . On a multi-GPU node, the total number of workers can become substantial. For example, eight training processes with 16 workers each can create 128 independent workers. Those workers may concurrently: Open and close files. Read file and directory metadata. Resolve paths and look up inodes. Issue data reads. Update access times, depending on mount options. The resulting workload is not simply a stream of large reads. It can also be a high-rate stream of small metadata operations. A simplified view of the I/O path PyTorch DataLoader workers Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 ... Worker N \ | | / \ | | / +-------+---------+--------------+ | v Linux Virtual Filesystem | +----------+----------+ | | v v ext4 XFS Block groups and Allocation groups journal coordination with per-AG metadata This is a conceptual diagram, not a claim that every operation is serialized by one global lock in ext4 or that XFS eliminates locking. Both filesystems use sophisticated concurrency mechanisms. The important distinction is that XFS can distribute many allocation and metadata operations across allocation groups. 2. Why ext4 can become a bottleneck ext4 is a mature filesystem. It performs very well across a wide range of workloads. Under highly concurrent metadata workloads, however, contention can arise around shared filesystem structures and journal activity. Two areas are worth understanding: Journal activity: metadata updates are coordinated through JBD2 transactions. A workload that creates, renames, or updates large numbers of files can generate substantial journal traffic. Allocation and metadata coordination: concurrent inode and block allocation can contend on shared structures, depending on the access pattern and filesystem layout. The practical point is not that ext4 has a single global mutex. It does not. Rather, the cost of coordinating metadata operations can become visible when many processes issue small, concurrent filesystem requests. 3. How XFS uses allocation groups XFS was designed for large filesystems and high-throughput workloads. One of its central design features is the allocation group (AG) . An XFS filesystem is divided into allocation groups. Each AG maintains its own allocation metadata, including structures used to track free space and inodes. These structures are commonly implemented using B+ trees. An allocation group maintains, among other things: Free-space information, indexed by block location and extent size. Inode allocation information. AG-local metadata and coordination structures. When multiple workers perform allocation or metadata operations, XFS can distribute work across different AGs rather than forcing all such activity through one shared allocation structure. This does not make XFS lock-free. It means its architecture provides multiple allocation domains, which can reduce contention for workloads that exercise them effectively. Practical implication: XFS is worth benchmarking when a node has many concurrent workers accessing a local NVMe filesystem, particularly when metadata activity is a measurable part of the bottleneck. 4. Checkpointing Saving a modern deep-learning checkpoint can involve writing tens or hundreds of gigabytes of tensor data. Examples include: PyTorch state dictionaries. Optimizer state. Distributed training or ZeRO partitions. BF16 or FP8 tensor dumps. The goal is to complete checkpoint writes quickly and predictably, minimizing the time training is interrupted or competing with storage activity. Extent-based allocation XFS uses extents to describe ranges of filesystem blocks. Instead of representing a file as a long list of individual block pointers, an extent can describe a contiguous range. For large sequential writes, this can keep file metadata compact and help the filesystem allocate large runs of blocks. The actual extent layout still depends on free space, concurrent activity, write patterns, and filesystem state; contiguity is not guaranteed. Delayed allocation With buffered I/O, XFS can delay choosing the physical blocks for newly written data until writeback. This gives the allocator more information about the write and can improve the chance of allocating larger, more contiguous extents. The allocsize mount option controls the default speculative preallocation size for buffered writes. It can influence allocation behavior, but it is not a guarantee that every write will be allocated in fixed-size chunks or that a checkpoint will consist of only a few extents. What about Btrfs and ZFS? Btrfs and ZFS provide valuable features such as snapshots, checksumming, and copy-on-write semantics. Those features can have costs for write-heavy workloads. For example, when data blocks are shared through reflinks or snapshots, modifying them can require copy-on-write allocation and associated metadata updates. Fragmentation and write amplification can become concerns in some workloads. However, it is too broad to say that every write on Btrfs or ZFS necessarily causes severe fragmentation or that every transaction causes problematic latency spikes. The outcome depends on workload, record and block sizes, pool or filesystem configuration, and the state of the storage. There is also an important XFS detail: XFS supports reflink-based copy-on-write when reflink is enabled and extents are shared. Ordinary, unshared file writes are not automatically copy-on-write. If the objective is a scratch filesystem with no need for reflink cloning, decide whether reflink support is useful before formatting the volume. 5. Filesystem comparison for deep-learning workloads The table below is a qualitative engineering guide, not a universal benchmark result. Actual performance depends on kernel version, filesystem configuration, device topology, dataset layout, and concurrency. Workload dimension XFS ext4 Btrfs / ZFS High-concurrency metadata activity Allocation groups can distribute allocation work Mature performance; contention depends on workload and layout More complex metadata paths; workload-dependent Large sequential checkpoint writes Extents and delayed allocation can help Generally capable of large sequential writes CoW and metadata behavior can add overhead in some configurations Small-file workloads Capable, but directory and inode behavior should be benchmarked Often competitive, especially for common directory workloads Performance varies with metadata and CoW workload Snapshots and cloning Reflink support is available when enabled No native filesystem snapshots or reflink equivalent Strong native snapshot / CoW feature sets Direct I/O and GPU-direct paths Supports direct I/O; GPUDirect Storage depends on the complete platform stack Supports direct I/O; GPU-direct support is platform-dependent Support and behavior depend on filesystem and platform Scratch-storage simplicity Strong option for large local volumes Strong general-purpose option Useful when CoW, snapshots, or checksumming are requirements Do not interpret this table as proof that XFS is always faster. Benchmark the access pattern that your training job actually uses. 6. The small-file caveat A common argument against XFS is that ext4 can perform very well with directories containing large numbers of small files. Consider a dataset containing: 1.2 million JPEG files, each around 20 KB. Several million WAV clips, each around 15 KB. In this scenario, directory lookup, inode access, path resolution, and file-open overhead can become a significant part of the input pipeline. But the more important design question is whether millions of individual files should be served directly to a multi-GPU training job in the first place. Every sample fetched through a loose-file layout may involve operations such as open() , metadata lookup, read() , and close() . At scale, those operations create kernel transitions and metadata-cache pressure that can limit throughput regardless of the filesystem. Anti-pattern class LooseAudioDataset ( torch . utils . data . Dataset ) : def __getitem__ ( self , idx ) : path = self . file_paths [ idx ] waveform , sample_rate = torchaudio . load ( path ) return waveform Better pattern import webdataset as wds dataset = ( wds . WebDataset ( "/mnt/fast_data/shards/train-{000000..000499}.tar" ) . decode ( "torch" ) . to_tuple ( "wav" , "cls" ) ) Instead of opening a separate file for every sample, the pipeline reads samples from larger sequential containers. Common options include: WebDataset / TAR shards HDF5 Zarr Memory-mapped Arrow LMDB A shard size in the range of hundreds of megabytes to a few gigabytes can be a useful starting point, but the right size depends on the number of workers, randomization strategy, storage capacity, and recovery requirements. Once data is packed into shards, the pipeline can perform larger, more sequential reads. That reduces per-sample metadata overhead and makes it easier to use the bandwidth of fast NVMe storage. 7. Production tuning guide for XFS on NVMe The following commands are starting points for a dedicated local scratch volume. They are not universal settings. Test them on the target kernel, NVMe device, and workload before deploying them on a production training node. 7.1 Format with an appropriate allocation-group count For example: sudo mkfs.xfs -f \ -d agcount = 32 \ -m reflink = 1,crc=1 \ -b size = 4096 \ /dev/nvme0n1 agcount=32 is an example, not a rule. More allocation groups do not automatically mean more performance. The appropriate count depends on filesystem size, CPU concurrency, and workload. Start with the mkfs.xfs defaults unless you have benchmark evidence that an explicit AG count helps. The example enables reflink support. If this is a scratch volume and you do not need reflink cloning, consider whether enabling it is necessary. Reflink support does not make every ordinary write CoW, but writes to shared extents do use CoW semantics. 7.2 Mount options An example /etc/fstab entry: UUID=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx /mnt/fast_data xfs noatime,nodiratime,logbufs=8,logbsize=256k,allocsize=64M,inode64 0 0 Review each option before applying it: Option Purpose Considerations noatime Avoids updating file access times on reads Often useful for read-heavy training data nodiratime Avoids directory access-time updates Generally redundant when noatime is active logbufs=8 Configures the number of in-memory log buffers More buffers are not automatically better; benchmark metadata-heavy workloads logbsize=256k Sets the log-buffer size Check the supported range for the running kernel and XFS version allocsize=64M Sets the default speculative preallocation size for buffered writes Test with the checkpoint write pattern; it is not a contiguity guarantee inode64 Allows inode allocation across the filesystem address space Commonly appropriate for large filesystems Do not copy mount options blindly. In particular, options such as logbufs , logbsize , and allocsize should be justified by measurements rather than treated as mandatory tuning. 7.3 Kernel and block-device tuning NVMe devices use multiple hardware queues. On many modern systems, the none I/O scheduler is a sensible baseline: # Inspect the active scheduler first cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler # Select the none scheduler echo none | sudo tee /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler For sequential shard reads, you can test a larger read-ahead value: # Example: 4096 sectors, typically 2 MiB with 512-byte sectors sudo blockdev --setra 4096 /dev/nvme0n1 You can also experiment with dirty-page thresholds: sudo sysctl -w vm.dirty_background_ratio=5 sudo sysctl -w vm.dirty_ratio=10 These settings affect system-wide writeback behavior. They can change when dirty pages are flushed and when processes are throttled; they do not guarantee that checkpointing will become faster. Test them under realistic concurrent training and checkpoint workloads, and make any persistent configuration changes deliberately. 8. Diagnosing storage bottlenecks Before changing filesystems or kernel parameters, establish what the storage path is actually doing. 8.1 Inspect checkpoint extent layout Use xfs_bmap to inspect the extent map of a checkpoint: xfs_bmap -v /mnt/fast_data/checkpoints/model_epoch_10.pt A large number of extents can indicate fragmentation, but extent count alone does not establish that fragmentation is hurting performance. Compare the layout with sequential read and write measurements. 8.2 Monitor device utilization and latency iostat -xz 1 /dev/nvme0n1 Pay attention to: rMB/s and wMB/s : observed throughput. await : average I/O wait time. aqu-sz : average queue size. %util : device utilization as reported by iostat . A device showing high utilization and low throughput may be handling many small or latency-sensitive requests rather than large sequential transfers. It can also indicate queueing, CPU limitations, or another bottleneck. Compare the results with the device's specifications and with a controlled benchmark; %util alone is not a reliable measure of NVMe saturation. 8.3 Profile CPU-side filesystem activity Use perf to identify where CPU time is going: sudo perf top You can also inspect XFS-related symbols and lock activity where available in your kernel's profiling environment. Symbol names and tracepoint availability vary by kernel, so first inspect the events exposed by the running system rather than assuming a particular event name exists. The goal is to determine whether the workers are spending meaningful time in filesystem metadata paths, block I/O, decompression, Python overhead, or data transformations. 9. Practical recommendations For a multi-GPU training node using local NVMe scratch storage: Benchmark XFS and ext4 with the real workload. Include both concurrent sample reads and large checkpoint writes. Prefer sharded datasets over millions of loose files. This often produces a larger improvement than changing filesystems. Use XFS when its allocation-group and large-file behavior fit the workload. Do not assume it wins every small-file or metadata benchmark. Treat mount and kernel parameters as experiments. Change one variable at a time and measure throughput, latency, CPU utilization, and training-step time. Measure the entire pipeline. GPU utilization is an outcome, not a diagnosis. Confirm that storage—not decoding, augmentation, Python, networking, or CPU scheduling—is the limiting factor. Conclusion For large local NVMe volumes serving concurrent deep-learning workloads, XFS is a strong filesystem candidate. Its allocation groups can help distribute metadata and allocation work, while extent-based allocation and delayed allocation are useful for large buffered writes. The biggest gains, however, usually come from treating storage as part of the training architecture. Shard datasets, measure metadata pressure, profile checkpoint behavior, and tune the filesystem against the actual access pattern. A well-designed input pipeline on a properly benchmarked filesystem is more valuable than a collection of aggressive mount flags. XFS is a good place to start—not a substitute for measurement.

title: I could not answer a basic question about my own training data
author: LXSAIHUB
summary: Someone asked me a simple question about a model I had put into production: where did the training data come from, and could I show that it was appropriate for what the system does. I had the architecture documented and the evaluation results written down. I did not have a clear, written account of the data itself. The answer lived in several places: a data-processing script, a folder naming convention, a note in a pull request, and my own memory. When I tried to write it down as a coherent account, I found gaps I had not noticed. Which sources were represented, which were thin, and whether any special-category data had slipped into a dataset. None of that was captured anywhere I could point to. So I built a starter that takes a plain description of how your AI system is trained or fed and turns it into an Article 10 data-governance draft. Art10Pack surfaces the themes in what you described, the places where your sources are thin or missing, and flags where special-category data may be present. It produces a draft to work from, not a verdict. Why Article 10 is a data question before it is a documentation question For high-risk systems under the EU AI Act, Article 10 deals with data and data governance. It concerns the training, validation, and test data: where it comes from, how it was collected and prepared, whether it is relevant and representative for the intended purpose, and how bias and errors are examined. It sits alongside other obligations for high-risk systems, including Article 9 on risk management, Article 12 on logging, and Article 14 on human oversight. Whether a system is high-risk at all is a separate classification question tied to the Annex III categories, and I am not going to pretend a text tool can settle that. What struck me is that this is mostly an engineering documentation problem. The obligation asks for an account of your data practices. Most teams have that knowledge distributed and undocumented. The hard part is not inventing a policy; it is noticing what you never wrote down. That is the narrow thing Art10Pack does. It reads your description, organizes it into themes, and marks the evidence gaps where the account is thin. The special-category flags point at where sensitive data may be involved, so you can go look. It is a structured prompt to check your own work. What the starter is, and is not A draft that looks official is easy to over-trust, so let me be exact. Art10Pack is decision-support. It is not legal advice, not a certification, and not a live audit harness. It does not connect to your data pipeline, inspect your actual datasets, or verify a single claim in your description. If you write that a source is licensed and representative, the draft reflects what you wrote. It will not check the license or measure representativeness. The output is a starter: themes, source gaps, and special-category flags built from the text you pasted. Its value is that it makes the gaps visible. An empty "source" section is a signal that you need to go find that information. A flag is a pointer to an investigation, not a finding. I would treat the whole document as a checklist of questions to answer with real evidence, not as the evidence itself. It also cannot decide whether your system is high-risk, whether a specific dataset satisfies Article 10, or whether you have met any obligation. Those determinations need someone who understands your system and the law. The tool maps the terrain; it does not certify the route. The trade-off I accepted I could have built something that inspects a real dataset and scores it. That is a much heavier tool, needs access to your data, and still cannot answer the legal question of whether your governance is adequate. It would also be useless at the stage where I most needed help, before the documentation exists at all. A pasted-description starter works at that stage, when noticing a missing source is cheap. That portability is the limit too. Garbage in, plausible-looking draft out. I built the tool for the failure I personally had: scattered knowledge nobody had assembled into a written account. It is good at making you assemble it. It is not good at telling you the assembled account is true. If your data governance lives in a script and a pull request, Art10Pack will at least get it onto one page so you can see what is missing. FAQ What is Art10Pack? A decision-support starter that turns a pasted description of how your AI system is trained or fed into an Article 10 data-governance draft with themes, source gaps, and special-category flags. Does it inspect my actual training data? No. It works from the text you paste. It does not connect to your pipeline, read your datasets, or verify your claims, and it is not a live audit harness. Can it tell me whether my system is high-risk or compliant? No. Classification under the EU AI Act and any determination of compliance are outside its scope. It is not legal advice and not a certification. What should I do with a source gap or a flag? Go find the real evidence. A gap means the account is thin; a flag means special-category data may be involved. Both are prompts to investigate, not findings.

title: Content-Length on Our API Host: 47 Answers Carry It, 4 Are Chunked, and gzip Flips Two More
author: OnePassApps
summary: I work on OnePassApps , the team behind app.onepassapps.com. This post is about something our own API host does that I had never measured as a set: how it tells a client how long the answer is. Everything here was measured on 10 November 2026, from outside the browser, signed out, plain HTTPS, no cookies and no JavaScript. The short version Our API host uses two different ways of telling the client how long the body is, and the split falls on the size of the answer. 47 of the 51 answers I fetched carry a Content-Length header. The other 4 arrive chunked, with no length at all. Route Body bytes How the length is sent /api 104 Content-Length: 104 /api/auth/config 371 Content-Length: 371 /api/health 410 Content-Length: 410 /api/runtime 471 Content-Length: 471 the 43 single-record product routes 374 to 464 Content-Length, and the number matches the body exactly /api/config/feature-flags 1,771 Transfer-Encoding: chunked /api/plans 4,020 Transfer-Encoding: chunked /api/voting 4,146 Transfer-Encoding: chunked /api/products 15,650 Transfer-Encoding: chunked The boundary sits between two measured values: the largest body that carried Content-Length was 471 bytes, and the smallest chunked body was 1,771 bytes. I did not find the exact byte where the server switches, so I am not claiming one. It is the uncompressed size that decides Here is the part that surprised me. I asked the same routes for a compressed copy, with Accept-Encoding: gzip. /api/runtime answered 471 bytes with a Content-Length of 471. Asked for gzip it answered 299, 301 and 301 bytes across three fetches, and switched to chunked. /api/health answered 410 bytes with a Content-Length of 410. Asked for gzip it answered 288, 289 and 287 bytes, chunked. So the smaller the body gets, the more likely it is to arrive with no length at all. The rule is not "small answers get a length". The rule is closer to: an answer that is produced in one piece and can be held in memory gets a length, and anything the server streams gets chunked. For the record, the two big routes stayed chunked when compressed: /api/config/feature-flags came back at 520, 523 and 524 gzipped bytes, and /api/products at 1,776, 1,777 and 1,778. A HEAD request still costs a token A HEAD request to our API routes answers 200 with a zero-byte body, the JSON content type and no length header at all. That part is not new. What is new to me is what it costs. I sent five HEAD requests to /api/products in a row, and the remaining-counter header fell by exactly one each time: 71, then 70, then 69, then 68, then 67. The next GET answered 66. A HEAD returns nothing, and it still spends a request from the same 120-request budget that a full GET spends. If a client is probing a list of routes to see which ones exist, those probes are billed like reads. What this measurement does not cover One build, one day, one network, one region, plain HTTPS, no cookies, no JavaScript, no session and no sign-in. I fetched 51 URLs: the 8 fixed routes under /api and the 43 single-record product routes the catalogue lists. I did not fetch the route behind a signed-in view. I sent one request per URL for the census and three requests each on the eight fixed routes to check the split was stable. I read the headers the server sent; there is a CDN in front of both hosts and I cannot see how it stores or rewrites what it receives. And every number here is a snapshot of one build on one day. Try it yourself The home page is where all nine apps are listed, and every one of them runs in your browser tab: the OnePassApps home page Every app and studio has a plain-language guide with its limits and its tool list: the OnePassApps guides

title: I kept shipping agents I had only tested on the happy path
author: LXSAIHUB
summary: The first test I write for a new agent is always the one it passes. A clean input, a well-formed tool response, a sensible final answer. I tell myself I will add the messy cases later. Later usually means after the first user finds them. The failure I kept hitting was not a crash. It was the quiet case: a tool returns an empty result, an instruction lands in a retrieved document, a user asks for something the agent has no tool for, and the agent improvises instead of saying it cannot. None of those show up in a single happy-path run. They show up in a batch. So I built a tool that runs an agent definition against a batch of simulated scenarios and reports what happened. You give it the definition, it generates scenarios, and it returns a success rate and a list of failure modes. AgentSim is a pre-release gate, the step between "it worked on my input" and "I am willing to ship it." The gap between one run and a batch A single run tells you almost nothing about an agent, because the input space is unbounded. The agent is a function over text, tool outputs, and whatever the model decides to do that day. Testing it once is like load-testing a server with one request. What I wanted before a release was a distribution, not a pass. Give me a batch of plausible situations, some clean, some adversarial, some malformed, and tell me how the agent behaves across them. Which categories of input does it handle, and which does it consistently mishandle. That is a question a batch can answer and a single run cannot. AgentSim generates the scenarios, runs the definition against them, and reports a success rate plus the failure modes it saw. The useful part is not the number; it is the grouping. "Handles missing tool output poorly across these cases" is actionable in a way that "one test failed" is not. I can look at that cluster and decide whether to add a guard, a fallback, or an explicit refusal path. What the simulation is, and is not "Simulation" invites overconfidence, so let me be careful. The scenarios are generated, not sampled from your production traffic. The tool does not run your agent against real users, real tools, or a live model deployment. It runs the definition against simulated cases. The success rate is a property of that batch, not a prediction of your uptime in the wild. That makes it a pre-release gate, not a certification. A gate answers a narrow question: does this definition fall apart on the cases we can think of before shipping. A certification would answer a much larger one: is this system safe in deployment. AgentSim answers the first. I would be misleading you if I let the word "safety" imply the second. Scenario generation has its own blind spot: it can only produce the kinds of situations it knows to produce. A novel failure mode no generated scenario resembles will not appear in the report. I treat the output as a floor on the problems, not a ceiling: everything flagged is worth fixing, and the absence of a flag is not proof of safety. Honest limits and the trade-off Here is the plain statement. AgentSim is a decision-support tool. It is not legal advice, not a certification, and not a live audit harness. It does not observe a running system, inspect real logs, or test your production integrations. It reads an agent definition and simulated scenarios, and reports a success rate and failure modes for that batch. I accepted that limit deliberately. A live evaluation harness that replays real traffic needs access to your environment and your data, and it only becomes useful after you have shipped. The moment I most needed a signal was before release, when a definition is cheap to change. A simulated batch fits that moment. It will not catch everything, but it reliably caught the class of bug I kept shipping: the unhandled edge case a single happy-path test never exercises. If your current release check is one manual run you did yourself, AgentSim will at least turn that into a batch and show you the shape of what fails. FAQ What is AgentSim? A pre-release gate that runs your agent definition against a batch of simulated scenarios and reports a success rate and failure modes. Are the scenarios based on my real users? No. They are generated, not sampled from production traffic. The tool does not watch a live deployment. Does a high success rate mean my agent is safe to ship? No. It describes that batch only. It is not a certification, not legal advice, and not a live audit harness. Novel failure modes the scenarios do not resemble will not show up. What should I do with the failure modes? Treat them as a floor, not a ceiling. Fix what is flagged, and do not read an empty flag list as proof of safety.

title: Metacognition Leaderboard for LLMs: JGENai VIDRAFT Launch a Benchmark That Measures Self-Error Detection, Not Just Accuracy
author: AI OpenFree
summary: Metacognition Leaderboard for LLMs: JGENai × VIDRAFT Launch a Benchmark That Measures Self-Error Detection, Not Just Accuracy TL;DR: JGENai and VIDRAFT have jointly released a metacognition benchmark, a 24-model public leaderboard, and 11 model-specific metacognition adapters designed to measure whether an AI can detect its own mistakes — not just whether it gets answers right. The adapters attach to existing models without modifying weights or architecture, making them drop-in reliability probes for high-stakes applications. Developers can explore the leaderboard, benchmark dataset, and adapters on Hugging Face. What it is JGENai (CEO Sunyoung Choi) and VIDRAFT have co-developed and publicly released three artifacts: A metacognition benchmark — 400 adversarial "trap" questions designed so the superficially plausible answer is wrong, testing whether a model can catch its own likely errors rather than just pattern-match to a confident-sounding output. A 24-model public leaderboard — ranking current Korean and multilingual LLMs on both multiple-choice accuracy and open-ended self-error-detection capability. 11 model-specific metacognition adapters — lightweight add-ons that sit beside a target model and assess the risk that any given response is incorrect, without touching the base model's weights. The core thesis: the dangerous moment for an AI is not when it's wrong, but when it doesn't know it's wrong. In domains like medicine, law, finance, security, and scientific research — where error costs are high — self-error detection is framed as a primary reliability signal, not an afterthought. How it works Benchmark design Each of the 400 benchmark problems is constructed so that one answer appears strongly plausible at first read, while the actual correct answer requires the model to pause and re-examine its own reasoning. Evaluation is split across two axes: Multiple-choice accuracy — standard answer correctness on trap questions. Open-ended self-assessment — after generating a free-form answer, can the model correctly judge whether that answer is likely wrong? This dual-axis design exposes a gap that single-accuracy leaderboards miss: a model can score well on axis 1 while being nearly blind on axis 2. Metacognition adapters The adapters are designed around a non-invasive attachment pattern: They do not modify the base model's architecture or trained weights. They analyze internal signals produced during the model's answer-generation process to compute a risk score indicating how likely the response is to be incorrect. The output is a separate risk signal — a flag or score that downstream systems, human reviewers, or orchestration layers can consume independently of the answer itself. This architecture means you can wrap an existing deployed model with a metacognition adapter without retraining, fine-tuning, or touching inference infrastructure beyond adding the adapter layer. Benchmarks & results From the publicly reported leaderboard results: JGOS-31B-Citizen ranked #1 out of 24 models evaluated. It answered 398 out of 400 trap questions correctly, achieving a 99.5% trap-avoidance rate . JGOS-31B-Citizen is also the current top-ranked model on the K-AI Leaderboard operated by Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) and the National Information Society Agency (NIA). Multiple models from the Darwin family (Darwin-28B, Darwin-31B, Darwin-35B) — all developed in Korea — placed in the upper tier of the leaderboard. Critically, models that performed strongly on multiple-choice accuracy still showed limited capability on open-ended self-assessment . This confirms that raw accuracy and metacognitive awareness are empirically distinct competencies — a model can be highly accurate yet unable to flag its own uncertain or incorrect outputs. How to try it The benchmark dataset, the 24-model leaderboard, and all 11 metacognition adapters are publicly available on Hugging Face . The source article does not specify exact repository slugs, so navigate directly to the JGENai organization page on Hugging Face to find the released artifacts. # Browse available artifacts via the Hugging Face CLI huggingface-cli scan-cache # Or search the JGENai org directly in your browser: # https://huggingface.co/JGENai No GitHub repository URL, API endpoint, or additional access mechanism was mentioned in the source article at time of publication. Check the Hugging Face model cards for adapter usage instructions specific to each of the 11 supported models. FAQ Q: Does applying a metacognition adapter require retraining or fine-tuning my existing model? A: No. The adapters are explicitly designed to leave the base model's weights and architecture unchanged. They attach externally and analyze generation-time signals to produce a separate risk score. Q: Is the benchmark only relevant for Korean-language models? A: The benchmark was developed with a Korean-language focus — the top-performing models are Korean LLMs — but the conceptual framework (trap questions + dual-axis evaluation) is language-agnostic. Whether English or multilingual models are included in the current 24-model leaderboard is not specified in the source article. Q: What does the risk signal from the adapter actually look like in practice? A: The source describes it as a computed probability that a given response is incorrect, derived from internal signals during generation. Exact output format (scalar score, binary flag, confidence interval) is not specified in the public reporting — check the Hugging Face model cards for implementation details. Q: Why does it matter that accuracy and self-error detection are separate skills? A: Because a high-accuracy model that cannot flag its own mistakes will confidently surface wrong answers in production with no warning. In regulated or safety-critical domains, that silent failure mode is often more dangerous than a lower-accuracy model that correctly signals uncertainty.
