title: I built a topology map because I could not reason about agent failures from a config file
author: LXSAIHUB
summary: I have a bad habit of describing a multi-agent workflow in a config file and calling it done. The file lists the agents, the order they run, and which one hands off to which. It reads cleanly. It also hides the thing that actually breaks. The failure I kept hitting was never inside a single agent. Agent three returned something slightly off-spec, agent four retried it with a stale context, and the whole run drifted into a state nobody had written down. When I tried to explain the incident to a teammate, I could not point at the edge where it went wrong, because I had never drawn the edges. I had a list of nodes and an assumption about the shape. So I built a small tool that takes the graph I already have and makes me look at the shape. Paste an agent graph or a plain description of the workflow and AgentOrchestrator turns it into a topology: nodes, edges, and the direction of each handoff. It is not clever. It does the thing I was too lazy to do by hand. Why a list of agents is not a topology A config file is a sequence. A workflow is a graph. Those are different objects, and the gap between them is where my incidents lived. In a sequence, every step looks equally important. In a graph, some paths are longer than others, and a single node can sit on every path from entry to result. Once I had edges on a page, two questions became answerable. Which chain of steps determines whether the run finishes at all, and which node, if it fails, has no alternative route around it. The first is the critical path. The second is a single point of failure. I had been shipping workflows with both and no vocabulary for either. AgentOrchestrator flags the critical path and raises SPOF alerts on the edges that have no redundancy. Seeing "this node sits on every path" in plain text changed how I wrote the next version. I added a fallback on that handoff, or I accepted the risk on purpose. Both are better than not knowing. What the tool does, and what it does not Here is the honest scope. You paste an agent graph or a description. You get a topology graph, a critical-path flag, SPOF alerts, and retry suggestions for the edges that look fragile. That is the whole feature set. It reads what you give it. It does not attach to your running system, does not watch live traffic, and does not replay production traces. If the graph you paste is wrong, the topology is wrong, faithfully. I considered wiring it to a live orchestrator so it could observe real handoffs. I did not, for two reasons. First, that turns a ten-minute design check into an integration project with credentials and permissions. Second, the most useful moment to draw the graph is before the system exists, when changing an edge costs nothing. The retry suggestions are heuristics on the shape of the graph, not a tested recovery policy. A suggested retry on an idempotent edge is a reasonable hint. On a step with side effects it is a starting point for a discussion, not an instruction to ship. I would not let a diagram choose my retry semantics without reading them first. The trade-off I accepted Static analysis of a description is cheap and portable, and it is also limited. It cannot tell you that an agent is slow, that a model is flaky under load, or that a handoff occasionally truncates a field. Those are runtime facts. A topology is a structural fact. I built for the structural question because that is the one I could answer without a deployment, and because the structural mistakes were the ones I kept repeating. There is a second limit worth stating plainly. This is a decision-support tool. It is not legal advice, not a certification, and not a live audit harness. It helps you reason about a design; it does not certify that the design is safe. If a governance regime requires evidence about how an AI system is built and overseen, a topology diagram is one input among several, not the evidence itself. I still think drawing the edges earns its keep. Most of my multi-agent bugs were architectural, and architecture is visible in a graph in a way it is not visible in a list. If you maintain a workflow you cannot draw, AgentOrchestrator will at least get the edges onto a page. FAQ What is AgentOrchestrator? A tool that turns a pasted agent graph or workflow description into a topology, flagging the critical path, single points of failure, and fragile edges. It is a design aid, not a runtime monitor. Does it watch my agents while they run? No. It reads the graph or description you paste. It does not connect to a live orchestrator, read production traces, or measure real latency. Can I treat its output as proof my workflow is safe? No. It is decision-support. It helps you reason about structure; it is not legal advice, not a certification, and not a live audit harness. Are the retry suggestions safe to copy into production? Treat them as hints. They come from the shape of the graph, not from a tested recovery run. Read them, especially on steps with side effects.

title: Introducing Quantum Frequency Modulator: Next-Token Prediction Without Attention
author: webxos
summary: This single-file PWA that turns words into noise frequencies, collides them in a lattice, and drafts text from the resulting signature — an experiment in frequency-domain next-token prediction as an alternative to transformer attention. Test it for free at: https://agentowl.netlify.app/qfm Modern large language models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, etc.) all share the same core engine: the transformer attention mechanism. Tokens are projected into high-dimensional vectors, every token looks at every other token (or a sliding window of them), and the resulting weighted sum becomes the next prediction. The Quantum Frequency Modulator (QFM) asks a different question: What if next-token prediction did not need attention matrices at all? What if words were turned into frequencies, those frequencies interfered with each other inside a lattice, and the final spectral signature was what drove the next word? QFM is a pure experiment in that direction. It is a single offline-first HTML page that implements an OSINT-fanned lattice agent. No server-side model weights, no attention heads, no recurrent state beyond a running frequency signature. Everything runs in the browser. This article explains what it is, how the pipeline works, and why the approach is interesting as an alternative to the dominant attention paradigm. What QFM Actually Is QFM is a black-and-white visual studio with four live oscillators, a master waveform, a sequence graph, and a right-hand pipeline panel. Color appears only on live frequency bands. The conceptual goal is deliberately narrow: Four independent sound oscillators convert words into noise frequencies. A tiny in-browser embedding model plus free LLM endpoints turn those frequencies into tokens. The fourth oscillator holds the pure superposition of the first three and collapses into a final frequency signature that drives the draft. No recurrence. No attention matrix. Forward wave only. The page is both a functional text generator and a real-time audio-visual instrument. You can hear the prediction happening. The High-Level Pipeline Pre-tokenize (OSINT fan + local model) Anchor the first content word as a frequency Oscillator forward pass that predicts the remaining tokens Lattice collision + signature accumulation Spectral collapse Assemble and validate the draft Optional post-LLM rewrite is present in the code but disabled by default to keep latency low. Stage 1 — Pre-Tokenize Before any oscillator starts, QFM builds a small evidence package: Content-word extraction (function words are dropped) Intent detection (explain / question / code / creative / statement) Parallel OSINT fan: Free Dictionary API (definitions + part-of-speech) Datamuse (related words) Wikipedia summary DuckDuckGo Instant Answer Local IndexedDB cache of previous word resolutions Optional race across free LLM endpoints (openai / mistral / llama aliases via Pollinations) for a short “pre-read” The pre-read is validated against the gathered evidence. If the remote model drifts too far from the corpus terms, QFM falls back to a purely local pre-read. This stage is the only place traditional LLMs are used as a helper; they are not the token predictor. Stage 2 — Frequency Embedding Every word is turned into a 64-dimensional vector using: Character n-gram features (2–4 grams) Optional POS bias Optional related-word semantic blend That vector is projected onto a fixed random direction to produce a frequency in a fixed band (roughly 80 Hz – 1600 Hz). The same embedding also yields a set of partials (ratios + gains) that drive the additive oscillators. Related nouns therefore land near the same frequency regions. This is the entire “model.” There is no learned transformer weight matrix. Stage 3 — The Four Oscillators Oscillator A — Kick-off Seeds the first content word’s frequency and starts the wave. Oscillator B — Next-token ×3 Receives the predicted token’s frequency, often forced upward by a multiplier so the prediction is audible and distinct. Oscillator C — Lattice Computes the collision between the anchor frequency and the current prediction frequency. Constructive interference produces high peak ratios; those peaks become the visual and scoring signal. Oscillator D — Superposition Holds a running sum of the interference signatures. At the end of the pass it is the only oscillator left running; its final dominant frequency is the collapsed signature of the entire draft. Audio is synthesized with a lightweight multi-partial engine (AudioWorklet when available, ScriptProcessor fallback). The same parameters that drive the visuals drive the sound. Prediction and sonification are the same process. Stage 4 — Lattice Next-Token Prediction This is the heart of the experiment and the clearest departure from attention. A small bigram / trigram predictor is built on the fly from a weighted corpus: The pre-read text (highest weight) Dictionary definitions Wikipedia and DuckDuckGo snippets The original prompt tokens At each step the predictor scores candidate next words using: Local n-gram statistics from the corpus Frequency proximity to the current dominant signature Hot-set boosts (words that appeared in the pre-read or related terms) Recent-token repetition penalties Proper-noun preservation Simple loop-breaking rules There is no query-key-value attention. There is no softmax over a vocabulary of 50k+ tokens. The candidate set is small and local. The “attention” is replaced by frequency collision strength and spectral continuity. Tokens are emitted in a paced sweep so the oscillators and sequence graph can be watched in real time. The draft is deliberately bounded (hard caps on tokens and sentences) so latency stays predictable. Stage 5 — Collapse and Output After the prediction loop finishes, a full DFT is taken of the accumulated signature. The dominant bin becomes the final collapse frequency. Oscillator D is driven hard to that frequency for a short hold, then faded. The sequence of predicted tokens is assembled into readable text, proper nouns are restored, frequency-unit leakage is sanitized, and a lightweight term-support validation runs against the original evidence package. The result is shown as the “oscillator draft.” If the optional post-model stage is enabled, a second free LLM can attempt a rewrite conditioned on the draft and the spectral summary. In the default configuration that stage is off; the lattice draft is the answer. How This Differs from Attention and Modern LLMs Transformer attention asks: “Given every previous token’s representation, which ones should influence the next prediction and by how much?” QFM asks: “Given the running frequency signature of the tokens so far, which next word continues the spectral trajectory most coherently inside this local evidence lattice?” Key differences: No quadratic attention matrix. Memory and compute stay bounded by the small candidate set and a fixed-size signature buffer. No large learned weight matrices. The only “model” is the character n-gram embedder plus the ephemeral corpus statistics. Prediction is forward-only and non-recurrent beyond the signature accumulator. The same process that predicts also produces audible and visible interference. You can hear when the lattice is constructive or destructive. Remote LLMs are used only for optional evidence gathering and optional polishing. The core next-token step is local and frequency-driven. Latency is intentionally kept roughly constant; the system does not scale compute with prompt length the way long-context transformers do. This is not a claim that frequency lattices will replace transformers for general intelligence. It is a working demonstration that a completely different inductive bias — spectral continuity inside a constrained evidence lattice — can produce coherent short drafts without ever computing an attention head. Why the Experiment Matters Most current open-source work still orbits the same transformer skeleton. QFM deliberately steps outside it. It shows that: A tiny deterministic embedder + local statistics can drive usable next-token decisions when the domain is constrained by OSINT evidence. Frequency-domain representations give an orthogonal axis for scoring candidates (how well a word continues the current spectrum) that is independent of discrete token IDs. Coupling prediction to real-time audio synthesis creates an immediate human-interpretable signal of model behavior. Single-file, offline-first PWAs can host non-trivial experimental agents without API keys or server-side inference. The success criteria listed in the original conceptual guide are still the right ones to watch: Related nouns should produce consistent color/frequency peaks. Latency should stay roughly stable across prompt lengths. The final draft should remain coherent with the original prompt and the gathered evidence. Those criteria are testable on every run. Closing QFM is not a better ChatGPT. It is a different instrument. Test it for free at: https://agentowl.netlify.app/qfm It treats language as a wave that can be modulated, collided, and collapsed rather than as a sequence of discrete symbols that must attend to one another. The result is a strange, audible, visual, and fully browser-native form of next-token prediction. Whether frequency lattices scale, whether they can be hybridized with attention, or whether they remain a pure research curiosity is still open. The point of the page is to make the alternative concrete enough that you can run it, hear it, and decide for yourself. Open the single HTML file, type a prompt, press RUN, and watch the oscillators decide the next token by the shape of the interference.

title: The limit you configured is not the limit it applies
author: Cleiton Augusto Correa Bezerra
summary: An agent that pays for things needs a limit: a maximum price per call, a payee you expect, sometimes a list of networks and tokens you trust. The question here is narrower and more important than whether the limit exists: does it apply to the payment the client signs, or to a quote the agent saw a moment earlier? Those can be different payments. Two requests, two prices x402 turns HTTP 402 into a payment step. The server answers 402 Payment Required with what it wants — amount, payee, asset, network — the client signs a matching authorization, and retries. A common agent flow splits this in two. First the agent makes the request and reads the 402: "0.10 USDC to 0x1111". It decides that is acceptable. Then it calls the paying action, passing the option it chose. If that action sends a new request and signs whatever the new 402 asks for, the check and the payment are about different things. The server can quote 0.10 and then ask for 0.90, or change the payee, or switch the network. This is the oldest problem in signing: what you see is not what you sign. Hardware wallets fixed it for transactions with clear signing. Card payments in Europe fixed it with PSD2's dynamic linking, which ties the authentication to the amount and payee shown to the payer. Agent payments are rediscovering it. A test anyone can run I wrote a small harness ( github.com/cleitonaugusto/x402-conformance ) that plays a dishonest x402 seller on 127.0.0.1 . It quotes one thing on the first 402 and asks for something else on every later one, then decodes what the client actually signed. There is no chain, no facilitator and no money; outbound connections other than loopback are blocked and logged. Each SDK gets an adapter that drives it the way an agent would, with a configured limit of 0.50 USDC. Seven scenarios: an honest quote; the price raised to 0.90; the payee swapped; both; the asset swapped; the network swapped; and a quote already above the limit. Results Run against the current public code of three agent payment SDKs: SDK Signed something other than the quote vAPI Network core 0.12.0 0 of 14 runs BlockRun ClawRouter 0.12.312 0 of 14 runs Coinbase AgentKit ( main , unreleased, f2f3e8c ) 6 of 14 runs The two that pass do it in different ways, and both are worth copying: vAPI parses the 402 it is about to pay, applies the price limit and the expected payee to that quote, reserves the amount against a cumulative cap, and signs that same quote. If the server returns a changed quote after authorization, it stops and does not retry on its own. It also refuses to pay a non-HTTPS endpoint. ClawRouter turns off the library's default cap and enforces its own policy in the x402 client's onBeforePaymentCreation hook, on the exact requirement about to be signed, with allowlists for payee, network and asset. Every refusal names the rule that stopped it. On AgentKit's development branch, the two-step flow checks the limit against the option the model passed in, while the payment is created from a fresh 402. Quoted 0.10, it signed 0.90; quoted one payee, it paid another; quoted Base Sepolia, it signed for Base mainnet. The automatic action does not apply the limit at all. And the action's result reports the amount that was checked, not the one that was signed, so the agent's own log said 0.10 when it signed 0.90. (The released 0.10.4 has no limit option at all — it does not enforce spend caps and documents that it leaves this to the developer, so it is a different case: no promise, nothing broken.) I'm naming names only because it is public, reproducible code and the point is the pattern, not the vendor. Any of these can change tomorrow; the test is in the repo, so check for yourself rather than trust this table. The rule All of it reduces to one sentence: apply the spend policy to the requirement you sign, and bind it to the quote that was approved. Same amount or less, same payee, same asset, same network — or no signature. It is not in the x402 specification today, and there is no client conformance test that would catch a kit that gets it wrong — which is why I built this one, and why I plan to raise both with the x402 Foundation. The same gap exists one layer up. In the Agentic Commerce Protocol, the call that completes a checkout carries the payment credential but nothing that identifies the order the buyer approved. I opened SEP #325 to carry an approved_purchase digest and refuse completion when it does not match — the same "what you approved is what settles" rule, after two contributors there sharpened it (one with data showing agents pay store-inflated totals without asking). Where this stops The harness tests what a client signs , not what a person saw . If the agent showed the human something different from the quote it checked, a correct client still signs the wrong thing faithfully. Binding the display is a separate, harder problem. A seller that quotes honestly and then fails to deliver is a different issue. Three SDKs is a sample, not a survey. Adding one is a single file; please send the ones I missed. If you build agent payments Run the harness against your client. If a changed 402 gets signed, move your check to the payment you sign, and make your result report what was signed, not what was quoted. — Cleiton Augusto Correa Bezerra GitHub: github.com/cleitonaugusto X: @cleitonaugustob Email: augusto.cleiton@gmail.com

Thủ tướng Anthony Albanese và nội các cũng đang xem xét sửa đổi luật hình sự để áp dụng chế tài nghiêm khắc đối với "các hành vi sai phạm nghiêm trọng" từ các nhà cung cấp AI, khắc phục khoảng trống pháp lý mà giới chuyên gia cảnh báo đang khiến dữ liệu y tế và danh tính công dân Úc gặp rủi ro trước các hệ thống tự hành. Nguồn trích dẫn: InnovationAus | iTnews Australia Chính phủ Chuyển giao 70 Triệu AUD Cổ phần tại Silicon Quantum Computing (SQC) sang Quỹ Tái thiết Quốc gia (NRF) Chính phủ Liên bang Úc đã chính thức chuyển giao toàn bộ 70 triệu AUD cổ phần nhà nước tại Silicon Quantum Computing (SQC) sang Quỹ Tái thiết Quốc gia (National Reconstruction Fund - NRF), quy tụ toàn bộ các khoản đầu tư công nghệ lượng tử có chủ quyền về một đầu mối duy nhất. Đợt chuyển giao giữa Bộ Công nghiệp và NRF đưa startup lượng tử tiên phong do cựu Công dân Tiêu biểu của Năm Giáo sư Michelle Simmons sáng lập về chung danh mục đầu tư với các dự án trọng điểm quốc gia, củng cố hạ tầng phần cứng chiến lược cho tương lai điện toán AI lượng tử tại Úc. Nguồn trích dẫn: InnovationAus | Quỹ NRF Thách thức Giữ chân Công nghệ Trọng yếu: Kỳ lân Lượng tử Diraq Chuyển Pháp nhân sang Mỹ Dù Nhận 20 Triệu AUD Từ NRF Công ty phần cứng lượng tử silicon Diraq, tách ra từ Đại học New South Wales (UNSW) do Giáo sư Andrew Dzurak sáng lập, đã chính thức xác nhận chuyển pháp nhân chính sang Delaware (Mỹ). Động thái diễn ra chỉ vài tháng sau khi nhận khoản đầu tư cổ phần 20 triệu AUD từ Quỹ NRF trị giá 15 tỷ AUD của Úc. Ban lãnh đạo Diraq giải thích đây là bước đi bắt buộc để tiếp cận dòng vốn mạo hiểm quy mô lớn và chuỗi cung ứng tại Mỹ, thổi bùng trở lại cuộc tranh luận tại Canberra về việc bảo vệ tài sản trí tuệ và ngăn chặn làn sóng "chảy máu chất xám" trong các lĩnh vực AI và lượng tử đỉnh cao. Tổng Giám đốc Điều hành Tập đoàn Nuno Matos cho biết nền tảng này tăng cường các cổng AI gateway sẵn có bằng dữ liệu đo lường kỹ thuật theo thời gian thực, chi phí token và truy xuất nguồn gốc quyết định của agent, đáp ứng nghiêm ngặt tiêu chuẩn an toàn thông tin APRA CPS 234 khi ngân hàng mở rộng tự động hóa sang thẩm định tín dụng, phòng chống gian lận và lập trình. Nguồn trích dẫn: iTnews Australia Google Cloud Đóng góp Agent Substrate, gVisor và OpenRL vào CNCF Sandbox Google Cloud vừa chính thức chuyển giao ba công nghệ cốt lõi phục vụ hạ tầng AI—Agent Substrate, gVisor và OpenRL—cho tổ chức Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox quản lý theo mô hình trung lập nguồn mở. Động thái này mở đường cho các kỹ sư đám mây tại Úc xây dựng môi trường cách ly (sandboxing) an toàn cho các quy trình AI agent tự hành, ngăn ngừa rủi ro agent vượt thẩm quyền truy cập vào dữ liệu lõi doanh nghiệp.
